topic.title: The Diwali box got lighter
topic.claim: When dry fruit prices double, the gift box doesn't get dearer, it gets lighter, because nobody weighs a gift.
topic.behaviour: Corporate buyers with fixed budgets cut the weight in the basket or swap in cheaper items. The box, the ribbon and the card stay the same. Seeds are showing up as gifts instead.
topic.mechanism: A gift is judged by how it looks when handed over. Weight and quality are invisible at that moment, so they are the first things to be cut.
topic.group: Working Indians who receive or send Diwali boxes at the office
topic.moment: The office Diwali box arrives and looks the same as last year, only it feels lighter in the hand.

turn.believed: A bigger price means a smaller gift is a visible loss.
turn.actually: The shrink happens inside the box, where nobody checks, and the packaging carries the rest.

topic.because: The buyer has a fixed budget and the receiver judges by appearance. So the smart move for the buyer is to cut what can't be seen. The sweet shops pass costs on openly, but the gift boxes do it silently.

proof.fact: Wholesale pistachios have gone from Rs 900 to Rs 1,800 per kg and dates from Rs 250 to Rs 500. Corporate gift buyers are working within fixed budgets, cutting basket weights or swapping in cheaper items.
Sweet prices in Hyderabad are up 20-25% ahead of Diwali, even though the Centre cut GST on nuts from 12% to 5%.

topic.payoff: Weigh the box next year. Nobody does, and that's exactly why it's the first thing to shrink.
topic.send_to: The colleague who always opens the box in the pantry and says 'last year it was bigger'
real_details: Demand for seeds as gifts has risen about 30% year on year, per CAIT's Shankar Thakkar.
A sweet-shop manager said 'We have no option but to pass on the increased costs to customers.'
Someone weighed a ₹5 Lay's packet with a gold weighing scale (they use it for clay miniatures) and found about 4.32g of chips, though the pack is marketed as 11+1.3g.
They said it was the lowest amount they had personally ever found in such a packet, and acknowledged it's only ₹5 but still felt cheated.
Another person asked why their KitKat had no wafer layers inside.
topic.news_peg: Reports on 2026-10-23 and 2026-10-25 showed dry fruit and sweet prices climbing before Diwali.
topic.why_now: Gift boxes are landing on desks this week.

score.why: The office Diwali box that feels lighter. The shrink happens where nobody checks, with dry humour.

Says more than the sources: 'Pistachio prices have doubled.'. What's true: Only one outlet, the Free Press Journal, reports a doubling, and that is for Mumbai wholesale/gifting pistachios against last Diwali. Economic Times (via FreshPlaza, 7 Oct 2026) reports in-shell pistachios up 60-74% year on year, not double. Telangana Today (25 Oct 2026) gives Hyderabad prices of about Rs 3,000-3,500/kg and does not report a doubling. A flat 'pistachio prices have doubled' is too broad. A safer wording is 'by one Mumbai trader account, pistachio prices roughly doubled from last Diwali', or 'up 60-70% or more'..

Says more than the sources: 'Wholesale pistachio prices went from Rs 900 a kilo to Rs 1,800 a kilo this year.'. What's true: The Free Press Journal says Rs 900 was the price 'last Diwali' and Rs 1,800 is the price now, and it calls these indicative trader prices. The claim says 'this year', which is not what the source says. The baseline is last Diwali (2025), not the start of this year. No second source confirms Rs 900 to Rs 1,800. ET/FreshPlaza gives wholesale in-shell at Rs 1,650/kg, up about 74% year on year. A 2025 Gujarat report put pistachios at Rs 1,050-1,200/kg, which conflicts with the Rs 900 baseline. The claim should be attributed to a Mumbai trader report and say 'since last Diwali'..
Could not verify: 'Mithai shops tell customers the new rate at the counter when prices rise.'. Cut it, or state it only if a source says it.
Could not verify: 'Next year's gift box will look the same as this year's but weigh less.'. Cut it, or state it only if a source says it.

mechanism.broken_premise: None fails outright, but two are overstated. (1) The price rise: the Rs 900 to Rs 1,800/kg figure matches the Free Press Journal's Mumbai trader quote, but ANI/ETV Bharat put the national rise at 60–70% (in-shell wholesale up about 74%). 'Doubled' is the top of the range, not a universal figure. (2) The budget: the reporting says 'most companies' work within fixed budgets. It does not say budgets cannot be stretched, and the same report says buyers are negotiating packages. The 'nobody checks' framing is also off. The buyer knowingly picks a lighter or seed-heavy hamper from the vendor, and retail pre-packaged boxes must state net weight on the label under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. Only the recipient doesn't see it. Custom or bulk corporate hampers may fall outside the retail labelling rules (I could not confirm that).
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Import disruption from Iran and Afghanistan (the US-Iran war), higher freight costs and a weaker rupee pushed Indian pistachio prices up roughly 60–100% before Diwali 2026. Most corporate gifting budgets are set per head, so buyers negotiate with hamper vendors. They take lighter baskets, swap costly nuts for cheaper items, and demand for seeds as gifting items is up about 30%. They do this rather than raise spend, so the per-unit price stays at the usual Rs 500–1,000 team tier while the grams of premium nuts fall. The cut is a deliberate, visible choice between buyer and vendor. It only looks hidden from the employee who receives the box.

Prices of in-shell pistachio have risen by 60-70% since Diwali 2025 ... Wholesale in-shell pistachio prices soared nearly 74% year-on-year ... The US-Iran war has impacted the imports of nuts and dry fruits from Tehran and Afghanistan.
Supplies from Iran and Afghanistan have been affected, while higher freight charges have increased the cost of bringing products to India.

_ledger.text:
[cover] Pistachio prices doubled. Your Diwali box just [got lighter].
Same box, same ribbon. Less inside.
 

[slide 1] Pistachio prices doubled. Your Diwali box just got lighter.
Swipe to read →

[slide 2] It's the week before Diwali. The box is on your desk when you get back from lunch.
Same gold cardboard and ribbon. Same printed card signed by leadership.
You pick it up to move it off your keyboard. Your wrist notices before you do.

[slide 3] You open it in the pantry. The cashews are still there, with room to roll around. Where the pistachios used to sit, there's a neat row of pumpkin seeds, now apparently a health choice.
Wholesale pistachios went from Rs 900 a kilo to Rs 1,800 this year. You'd expect the gift to cost more or look smaller.

[slide 4] But whoever orders the boxes is working within a fixed budget. They can't stretch it. And you judge the box in the two seconds it takes to land on your desk.
So the cut goes inside, where nobody checks.
The mithai shop at least tells you the new rate at the counter. The gift box says nothing.

[slide 5] You still type "thank you for the lovely gift 🙏" in the team group. Then a row of thumbs and diyas follows yours.
Somewhere in that row is the person who picked the pumpkin seeds.

[slide 6] Put this year's box on the kitchen scale before you open it. Write the number on the back of the card.
Next Diwali the box will look exactly the same. The scale won't.

[end card] Come back to this when next year's box lands on your desk.
The colleague who opens the box in the pantry and says 'last year it was bigger'

[caption] The mithai shop tells you the new rate at the counter. The gift box just hopes you don't own a kitchen scale.

[alt text] A six-slide carousel about office Diwali gift boxes. Pistachio prices doubled, so the box looks the same but holds less, with cheaper items like pumpkin seeds in place of pistachios. The buyer works within a fixed budget and you judge the box by how it looks when it arrives, so the cut happens inside where nobody checks. Everyone still thanks the team in the group chat. It ends by suggesting you weigh this year's box and write the number down, because next year's will look the same but weigh less.

A safer wording is 'by one Mumbai trader account, pistachio prices roughly doubled from last Diwali', or 'up 60-70% or more'.

c2.correct: The Free Press Journal says Rs 900 was the price 'last Diwali' and Rs 1,800 is the price now, and it calls these indicative trader prices. The claim says 'this year', which is not what the source says. The baseline is last Diwali (2025), not the start of this year. No second source confirms Rs 900 to Rs 1,800. ET/FreshPlaza gives wholesale in-shell at Rs 1,650/kg, up about 74% year on year. A 2025 Gujarat report put pistachios at Rs 1,050-1,200/kg, which conflicts with the Rs 900 baseline. The claim should be attributed to a Mumbai trader report and say 'since last Diwali'.

sources.quote: Pistachios, which were selling at around Rs 900 per kg last Diwali, now cost Rs 1,800 per kg.
Wholesale in-shell pistachios are US$18.37/kg, based on ₹1,650/kg.

c7.correct: No source I found says mithai shops tell customers the new rate at the counter. Telangana Today quotes a sweet-shop manager saying costs are passed on to customers, and that is all it says on the point. The claim is a generalisation with no support.

c8.correct: This is a prediction about next year's gift box, and no source supports it. The Free Press Journal reports only that corporate buyers are cutting basket weights or quantities this year, and it says nothing about next year or about boxes looking the same. Rewrite it as something already reported, such as 'some corporate buyers are cutting basket weights this year'.

sources.quote: corporate companies are reducing gift basket quantities and considering seeds as more affordable alternatives

mechanism.broken_premise: None fails outright, but two are overstated. (1) The price rise: the Rs 900 to Rs 1,800/kg figure matches the Free Press Journal's Mumbai trader quote, but ANI/ETV Bharat put the national rise at 60–70% (in-shell wholesale up about 74%). 'Doubled' is the top of the range, not a universal figure. (2) The budget: the reporting says 'most companies' work within fixed budgets. It does not say budgets cannot be stretched, and the same report says buyers are negotiating packages. The 'nobody checks' framing is also off. The buyer knowingly picks a lighter or seed-heavy hamper from the vendor, and retail pre-packaged boxes must state net weight on the label under the Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities) Rules, 2011. Only the recipient doesn't see it. Custom or bulk corporate hampers may fall outside the retail labelling rules (I could not confirm that).
mechanism.actual_mechanism: Import disruption from Iran and Afghanistan (the US-Iran war), higher freight costs and a weaker rupee pushed Indian pistachio prices up roughly 60–100% before Diwali 2026. Most corporate gifting budgets are set per head, so buyers negotiate with hamper vendors. They take lighter baskets, swap costly nuts for cheaper items, and demand for seeds as gifting items is up about 30%. They do this rather than raise spend, so the per-unit price stays at the usual Rs 500–1,000 team tier while the grams of premium nuts fall. The cut is a deliberate, visible choice between buyer and vendor. It only looks hidden from the employee who receives the box.

cover.sub: Same box, same ribbon. Less inside.

paragraphs: Dry fruit got dearer. Your Diwali box just got lighter.
slides.why_swipe: How does a box get lighter without anyone noticing?

paragraphs: It's the week before Diwali. The box is on your desk when you get back from lunch.
Same gold cardboard and ribbon. Same printed card signed by leadership.
You pick it up to move it off your keyboard. Your wrist notices before you do.
You open it in the pantry. The cashews are still there, with room to roll around. Where the pistachios used to sit, there's a neat row of pumpkin seeds, now apparently a health choice.
slides.why_swipe: Why would anyone swap pistachios for seeds?

paragraphs: Mumbai traders say wholesale pistachios went from Rs 900 a kilo last Diwali to Rs 1,800 now. You'd expect the gift to cost more or look smaller.
slides.why_swipe: It did neither, so where did the price go?

paragraphs: But whoever orders the boxes has a fixed budget. It doesn't stretch. And you judge the box in the two seconds it takes to land on your desk.
**So the cut goes inside, the one part you can't see from your chair.**
Sweet shops in Hyderabad raised prices 20-25% and said so out loud. The gift box changed its weight and said nothing.
slides.why_swipe: And what does everyone do about it?

paragraphs: You still type "thank you for the lovely gift 🙏" in the team group. Then a row of thumbs and diyas follows yours.
Somewhere in that row is the person who picked the pumpkin seeds.
slides.why_swipe: So how would you ever catch it?

paragraphs: Put this year's box on the kitchen scale before you open it. Write the number on the back of the leadership card.
**Nobody weighs a gift. That's exactly why the weight goes first.**

end.save: Come back to this when next year's box lands on your desk.
end.send: The colleague who opens the box in the pantry and says 'last year it was bigger'
end.promise: How things really get sold to you.

draft.caption: The ribbon got the full budget this year. The pistachios got the pumpkin seeds.
draft.alt_text: A seven-slide carousel about office Diwali gift boxes. Dry fruit got more expensive this year, with Mumbai traders saying wholesale pistachios went from Rs 900 a kilo last Diwali to Rs 1,800. The office box looks the same but feels lighter, with pumpkin seeds where pistachios used to be. The buyer has a fixed budget and you judge the box by how it looks when it arrives, so the cut happens inside, the part you can't see. Sweet shops in Hyderabad raised prices 20-25% openly, while the gift box changed silently. Everyone still thanks the team in the group chat. It ends by suggesting you weigh this year's box and write the number down, because a gift never gets weighed and that's why the weight goes first.

claims.text: Mumbai traders say wholesale pistachios went from Rs 900 a kilo last Diwali to Rs 1,800 now.
Corporate gift buyers are working within fixed budgets, cutting basket weights and swapping in cheaper items such as pumpkin seeds.
Cashews remain comparatively competitively priced, so they stay in the box.
Sweet shops in Hyderabad raised prices 20-25% before Diwali and say they are passing the higher costs on to customers.
